title: Crest V Ardmore: Blo Appeal In The English Courts Derailed By Insolvency? - JD Supra
content:
This is an important decision and those interested in this area of the law should keep track of the outcome of the CVA arrangements and whether the Court of Appeal gets to consider the case. The case of Crest Nicholson Regeneration Ltd v Ardmore Construction Ltd[1] has attracted significant commentary as essential reading for those looking to understand the reach of a 'Building Liability Order' (BLO) under the Building Safety Act 2022 (BSA). The interest was set to continue as Ardmore was granted permission to appeal by the Court of Appeal, with a date set for the hearing in December 2026. Unfortunately, those of us who were eagerly anticipating the judgment could be disappointed as the prospect of the appeal has been thrown into doubt due to several companies in the Ardmore group entering into Company Voluntary Arrangements (CVAs). Ardmore Construction Ltd (ACL) was engaged by Crest Nicholson (Crest) to design and construct 19 residential buildings at Admiralty Quarter in Portsmouth. Post-Grenfell investigations revealed extensive fire safety defects. Crest obtained an adjudication award of approximately £14.9 million, but ACL entered administration the day before the decision was issued. Crest sought two BLOs against associates in ACL’s group: an “anticipatory BLO” (extending any relevant liability ultimately established against ACL to certain associated companies) and an “adjudication BLO” (making the associates jointly and severally liable for the £14.9 million award). On 1 April 2026, Mr Justice Constable granted both. The Court held that: In a subsequent hearing on 8 May 2026 the BLO Defendants sought permission to appeal on five grounds. Mr Justice Constable refused permission on all of them and also refused a stay of execution and declined to certify the case for a leapfrog appeal to the Supreme Court, considering it a matter for the Court of Appeal. On the discretion point, Mr Justice Constable held that the threshold for appellate intervention is that the decision was “plainly wrong” (a very high hurdle) and the defendants had not cleared it. On the anticipatory BLO jurisdiction, the Court noted that accepting the argument would mean there could in practice never be such a thing as an anticipatory BLO. On the remaining grounds, the appellants had largely failed to engage with the reasoning of the original decision and had instead attempted to re-run arguments already advanced at first instance. The stay of execution also failed. The Court criticised the defendants’ financial evidence as inconsistent and incomplete, noting that the group chairman’s “reported (and not refuted)” personal fortune was more than sufficient to enable the group to continue trading. The Court of Appeal commended Mr Justice Constable's "comprehensive and closely reasoned judgment". They also observed that the applicants, Ardmore, "face a formidable challenge in seeking to appeal the Judge's conclusions on a decision which is rightly characterised as, in many respects, a form of statutory discretion". However, permission to appeal was granted on 9 June 2026, with expedition given the importance of the issues. A hearing is currently set for 15 December 2026. Ardmore argued that the appeal raises “issues of wider public importance for the construction industry, including the circumstances in which a Building Liability Order may be made and the extent to which liabilities may be imposed on group companies in respect of historic projects.” In line with this interpretation, the Court of Appeal noted that the issues raised by the appeal are "issues on which guidance from the Court of Appeal would be of real value". Two days after leave to appeal was granted, the wider Ardmore construction group entered administration, with the property arm applying for a Part A1 moratorium under the Insolvency Act 1986 to ensure protection from creditors and continue pursuing the appeal. The group has stated that the judgment affected client confidence and payment terms across live projects, materially impairing its ability to trade. This is now reflected by the entry into CVAs of members of the Ardmore group. In principle, a defendant may continue to pursue an appeal despite entering into a CVA. In practice, however, context is everything. This is not a case involving a single defendant. Five of the seven Ardmore group companies against whom BLOs are sought have entered into a CVA. Crest, as an unsecured judgment creditor, is bound by the full and final and binding terms of a CVA. The remaining two BLO Defendants are in administration. The insolvency proceedings raise questions about whether this appeal will be heard. That would be a significant loss for the construction industry. Crest v Ardmore was poised to provide greater certainty on the reach of BLOs, the availability of anticipatory orders, and the circumstances in which group companies can be held liable for the defaults of insolvent affiliates. While the BLO Defendants would have faced an uphill struggle, the Court of Appeal’s willingness to grant permission to appeal reflects the significant policy questions under scrutiny - questions that may now remain unanswered for the time being at appellate level. title: The architecture of persuasion: United States v. Hemani - SCOTUSblog
content: Although some law professors make a living hiding the ball, I will repeat my thesis right up front: Good legal writers are simply good writers – strong English stylists. As my first example, I offered Chief Justice John Roberts, who showed in Learning Resources v. Trump how to choose the optimal subject for English-language storytelling: an actor who can do things (there, the president imposing tariffs unlawfully). To emulate Roberts, focus on the first seven or eight words of your sentences in search of a subject that is a character. But why focus on those first seven or eight words? After all, subjects are moveable. As Master Yoda might say, “Near the end of a sentence, a subject you can find.” In United States v. Hemani, Justice Neil Gorsuch shows why we don’t write like Yoda speaks: English readers look for and prefer an early subject/verb transition, after which they will automatically emphasize new or important information at the end of a sentence. Gorsuch leveraged this tactic right in the first paragraph of Hemani, where he signaled (without saying so) that the Supreme Court had reached a surprising result. Remember back to October 2025 when the court granted certiorari. The cognoscenti (including my favorite legal podcast) predicted that Hemani would lose. Hemani seemed like other cases where a “bad man” (who smokes weed and might be a terrorist) goes to jail – at least until Gorsuch wrote his story. With sentence-level choices, Gorsuch immediately revealed that Hemani would prevail. We read that Hemani used marijuana “a few times a week.” But based on that fact alone, the government sought to “disarm him for life.” With this windup, Gorsuch asked whether this was “consistent with the Second Amendment.” Gorsuch made the outcome seem inevitable by placing each of the phrases quoted above at the end of a sentence. Even more, he placed all the key, persuasive information in the same position. Just like the chief in Learning Resources, Gorsuch is not engaged in legal writing so much as strong English style. From outside the legal academy, both George Gopen and Joseph Williams would tell you that English readers give the last few words of a sentence special emphasis. Gopen even calls them a “stress position.” And Gorsuch treats those stress positions as the most valuable real estate in an English sentence: Only key facts that drive the outcome are welcome to reside there. Focus on the sentence endings and you’ll see the facts crucial to Mr. Hemani. You’ll learn that Hemani spent “most of his life [in Texas].” He held a “stable job.” But the government searched the “family home in 2022.” When interviewed, Hemani was “cooperative.” He admitted using marijuana “about every other day.” Do the same thing, focus only on sentence endings, and you’ll see the factors that damage the government’s case. For example, the government did not prosecute Hemani for “terrorism—the reason for the search in the first place.” Nor did it prosecute him for “anything like [serious drug crimes].” Instead, he was charged merely as an “’unlawful user’ of a controlled substance.” Based on this alone, the government sought “disarmament for life” without contending Hemani was a “drug addict,” a “danger to himself or others,” or that he had done anything with his gun “other than possess it in his home.” To engineer those stresses, Gorsuch again makes an architectural choice that your English teacher would applaud: early subject/verb location. In “Style: Lessons in Clarity and Grace,” Williams notes, “If you have managed your subjects and topics well, you will by default put the words you want to emphasize toward the ends of your sentences.” He recommends curt beginnings: a short transition, a concrete subject, and a verb. And in “The Sense of Structure,” Gopen warns that your reader expects a subject to be followed “almost immediately” by the verb. With very few exceptions, Gorsuch used this architecture, putting his subjects and verbs together, right at the start of his sentences in Hemani. Indeed, he gets so snappy that several sentences rely on implied subjects that readers must supply on their own. (“No matter that the government did not assert Mr. Hemani was a drug addict. No matter that it did not contend that his drug use had ever led him to pose a danger to himself or others.”) In his factual narrative, Gorsuch made this choice in every sentence but four – and those were not an accident. Every time that Gorsuch significantly delayed subject and verb, he filled his initial, dependent clause with information that he thought should not change the outcome: gun ownership, uncharged crimes, and marijuana use. With this choice, a Jedi-level writer is signaling, “These aren’t the droids you’re looking for. Move along.” Thus, by intentionally delaying subject and verb, Gorsuch decreased reader attention on information that had no place in his persuasive mission. But a writer changes that story – perhaps drastically so – if subject and verb are placed haphazardly. Skeptical? Note how some versions of the same information undermine Gorsuch’s persuasive mission when Gorsuch’s own ideas are just moved around. In the first, Mr. Hemani’s work ethic is swallowed in a long, dependent clause, while the reader is invited to focus on the city where he lives. In the second, the work ethic becomes episodic and is swallowed between subject and verb, while the reader is invited to focus on a grown man living with his parents. But Gorsuch puts the emphasis where it helps his persuasive mission: Mr. Hemani works a stable job. Which Hemani would you rather be? The one who worked a stable job? The Dallas resident? Or the one who failed to launch and probably lives in his parents’ basement? So, to calibrate what your reader notices, write like Gorsuch. Prefer subjects and verbs together, near the beginning of a sentence. When you do, you help ensure that the most important information lands in the stress position where your reader will value it. Write first drafts in any style, even intuitively or by ear. But when you line edit, make structural decisions like an architect: Hemingway was right, so right that he now seems cliché. “Prose is architecture, not interior decoration, and the Baroque is over.” But if he has become cliché, that’s only because he has been right for so long. Sure, some lawyers and professors still primp ornamented, filigreed sentences. But English readers prefer a different architectural style: subject/verb . . . stress position. In Hemani, Gorsuch followed the blueprint. Professor Gray teaches legal writing courses for first-year and advanced students at Duke Law. title: Robert V. Miller Obituary Sep 10, 2026 - Timothy A. Berkebile Funeral Home, Inc.

title: People Not Politicians v. Onder (Amicus) - American Civil Liberties Union
content: Amicus Curiae Brief A “friend of the court” or amicus, brief is filed by someone not a direct party to the case, but who has an interest in its outcome. These briefs seek to supplement the merits briefs by offering the Court additional arguments and information. Amicus briefs can be filed at the merits stage or at the certiorari stage. Whether congressional elections in Missouri for the November 2026 midterms will be held using districts that never lawfully took effect because they have not been subject to a vote by the people via the referendum process. By completing this form, I agree to receive occasional emails per the terms of the ACLU's privacy statement. The ACLU, the ACLU of Missouri, and the Campaign Legal Center filed an amicus brief in People Not Politicians v. Onder in the U.S. Supreme Court, urging the Court to stay a temporary restraining order issued by a federal district court requiring Missouri to use a congressional map that has not lawfully taken effect. Missouri has eight congressional districts, one of which has historically been based in the Kansas City area. In direct response to partisan calls to gerrymander congressional districts before the 2026 midterm elections, Missouri engaged in mid-decade redistricting and passed HB 1, which seeks to dismantle Kansas City-based Congressional District 5. HB 1 would crack the city into three pieces and split them between three rural districts. This fracturing of Kansas City would prevent the area’s residents from uniting to have their voices heard by a single member of Congress. The redraw of the lines around Kansas City was along racial lines—and is aimed at unseating one of the two Black members of Congress representing Missouri. In one highly populated area of Kansas City, the new lines bisect Black and white neighbors, literally placing different racial groups on opposite sides of the track. After HB 1’s passage by the Missouri legislature in September 2025, more than 300,000 Missourians signed a referendum petition, as part of a campaign organized by People Not Politicians and Richard Von Glahn, to force the State of Missouri to put HB 1 to a vote by the people. A referendum would suspend HB 1 and prevent it from taking effect unless and until the people of Missouri approve the referendum. That would ensure that the midterm elections in November 2026 could be held using the districts in effect before Missouri’s mid-decade gerrymandering. Missouri’s Secretary of State, however, refused to determine whether the referendum petition was legally sufficient, until one hour before the statutory deadline of 5:00 p.m. on August 4, 2026, when he issued a finding that the referendum petition was insufficient, arguing that the Missouri Constitution does not authorize referenda on congressional redistricting plans. Mr. von Glahn, an organizer and signatory of the referendum petition signers, filed suit in Missouri state court that same day arguing that the Secretary violated state law and that he should be restrained from implementing, using, or mandating HB 1. The Missouri Supreme Court agreed with Mr. von Glahn and held that HB 1 must be subjected to the referendum process and that it cannot be used for the midterm elections in November 2026. The State sought a stay from the U.S. Supreme Court, which denied the request on September 8, 2026. Less than an hour after the U.S. Supreme Court’s ruling, a federal judge in the Eastern District of Missouri entered a temporary restraining order in Onder v. Missouri, enjoining the Secretary from implementing any congressional plan except HB 1. Richard Von Glahn and People Not Politicians sought a stay of the district court’s order before the U.S. Supreme Court On September 9, 2026, the ACLU, ACLU MO, and the Campaign Legal Center filed an amicus brief in support of the stay application in the U.S. Supreme Court. The brief argued that under longstanding federal precedent, the federal Elections Clause does not exempt redistricting legislation from the state's lawmaking process, including referenda, and that the Purcell principle foreclosed relief at this juncture, particularly given the confusion caused by the district’s court order, which had left the State of Missouri with no usable congressional districts on the eve of ballot mailing. The next day, the U.S. Supreme Court granted a stay of the district court’s order, which confirms that the State of Missouri must now implement the congressional districts as they existed before the 2025 gerrymander. Thus, Missouri’s 2022 congressional redistricting plan remains in effect, protecting the congressional district in the Kansas City area where voters have been electing candidates of their choice to Congress for over 100 years.

content: BOSTON, Massachusetts — The National Health Law Program (NHeLP), the Center for Public Representation, and 69 additional organizations filed an amicus brief today in Massachusetts v. Oz, detailing how the Trump administration’s Medicaid work requirements rule will strip health coverage from people with serious illnesses and disabilities. The brief supports the plaintiff states’ motion for partial summary judgment, which argues that the administration’s Interim Final Rule unlawfully narrows the exemption Congress created for people who are medically frail or have special medical needs. CPython Officially Adds RISC-V Support as a Tier 3 Platform Sep 10, 2026
								
								
								
									
									2
									min read The Python core development team has announced that the open instruction set architecture RISC-V is now officially supported by CPython as a Tier 3 platform. The announcement was shared on the Python Insider blog by contributor Stan Ulbrych, following sustained efforts across the community to stabilise and validate the implementation on real silicon. Reaching official inclusion in PEP 11, Python’s platform support document, required extensive collaborative work. Contributors spent months running tests on real physical hardware, resolving architecture-specific bugs, strengthening the build infrastructure, submitting patches, and reviewing changes. Ulbrych specifically highlighted hardware backing from the RISE Project, which provided multiple physical RISC-V machines to serve as buildbots for running automated tests and debugging architecture-specific problems. While Tier 3 designation marks a critical step forward, significant development remains underway. Buildbots typically execute tests only after a patch lands, which introduces latency when identifying defects. To address this, the team is working with the RISE Project through their RISE RISC-V Runners initiative to introduce RISC-V hardware directly into CPython’s continuous integration pipeline, offering contributors faster automated feedback. Looking further ahead, maintainers plan to advance RISC-V toward Tier 2 support within PEP 11. Core contributors also aim to investigate architecture-specific optimisations that unlock higher runtime performance by taking better advantage of RISC-V platform capabilities. To validate stability across diverse setups, the development team has issued an explicit call for testing from developers with access to compatible boards. Ulbrych noted: "Importantly, we need people to use it and give us feedback. If you have access to RISC-V hardware, please try building and running CPython, run your workloads and test suites, and please let us know what breaks." Finally, Ulbrych emphasised that CPython represents only a single layer of the broader ecosystem. Expanding full RISC-V viability will rely on ongoing community contributions across third-party Python packages, compilers, toolchains, and developer infrastructure. Community discussions on Hacker News and Reddit’s RISCV community welcomed the milestone as a vital maturity signal, while actively dissecting the practical engineering implications of a Tier 3 designation. Developers noted that while Tier 3 status means the platform can still occasionally experience breakage without blocking core releases, official upstream support removes a major historical friction point for integrating RISC-V into software CI/CD pipelines. Conversations also centred around hardware profiles like RV64GC and upcoming standards like RVA23, exploring how modern core capabilities, such as vector extensions, bit manipulation, and branchless instructions, could eventually be leveraged to optimise Python interpreter performance. RISC-V represents an open-standard instruction set architecture designed to provide an alternative to proprietary counterparts like x86 and ARM. Unlike x86, which is proprietary and closely guarded by legacy commercial entities, or ARM, which operates under restrictive licensing fees and strict corporate control, RISC-V is developed as an open standard that anyone can implement. Because its specification is fully accessible and modular, the surrounding ecosystem has expanded considerably in recent years, with industry projections estimating it will quadruple by 2032. This openness eliminates vendor lock-in, avoids proprietary licensing barriers, and provides a customizable, royalty-free hardware foundation for modern computing. Ensuring Python operates reliably across these systems has consequently become a major priority for the language ecosystem. title: ‘Bush v. Gore’ in Missouri? Congressional map showdown pits state law against federal law - KFVS12
content: JEFFERSON CITY, Mo. (Heartland News) - A “battle of the maps” is ensuing in the Show Me State as the nation’s eyes turn to a highly anticipated Missouri Supreme Court hearing Thursday morning. Missouri’s state courts and federal courts are locked in a historic jurisdictional standoff over which congressional map will govern the upcoming midterm election. The tension has escalated so far that the state’s highest court has ordered Secretary of State Denny Hoskins to return to Jefferson City immediately to explain in person why he should not be held in contempt of court. Political analysts liken the showdown to the 2000 election and Bush vs. Gore. This November’s midterm election will be closely watched as the balance of power in Congress could shift. Missouri’s congressional map could make the difference of one seat for either the Republican or Democratic party in the U.S. House of Representatives. The map in question decides who represents Missourians in the U.S. House of Representatives. Missouri lawmakers drew a new congressional map during a special session last year. The 2025 map carves up the Kansas City area into three districts, creating a map that favors sending a Republican to Washington D.C. over current Democratic Congressman Emanuel Cleaver. This was part of a national redistricting back-and-forth between Republicans and Democrats as the 2026 midterm election could change the balance of power in the U.S. House. A veto petition challenging the map gathered more than 300,000 signatures. If approved, the petition would put the 2025 map on pause, revert voters to the map drawn in 2022, and put a question on the November ballot for voters to decide which map to use going forward. Secretary of State Denny Hoskins rejected that petition on the same day as the August primary election, leading to the state lawsuit. The primary election was conducted under the new 2025 map, although a previous ruling from the Missouri Supreme Court said that map would have never gone into effect if the petition was found to have enough valid signatures. The conflict centers on two competing maps. The Missouri Supreme Court ruled that the state must use the 2022 congressional map for the upcoming election, tossing out a new map drawn last year to favor Republicans (HB 1). However, a federal district judge subsequently issued a Temporary Restraining Order (TRO) enjoining Hoskins from using any map other than the Republican-drawn HB 1 map, citing federal constitutional and equal protection grounds for voters who already voted in the primaries under those boundaries. Following the federal order, Hoskins immediately instructed local election clerks to proceed with the HB 1 map. Hoskins was at the airport Wednesday, cutting his trip to the Republican National Convention in Dallas short to be back in Missouri for the state court hearing Thursday morning. Speaking at the airport, Hoskins defended his decision by invoking federal supremacy. “The Supremacy Clause, where if you read Article 6 Clause 2 of the US Constitution, it basically says where federal law and state law conflict, the federal wins,” Hoskins said. When asked about the ongoing legal drama, Hoskins insisted he did his job properly. “I would say I met every state law deadline, I met every constitutional deadline,” Hoskins said. “There’s a reason we have deadlines and I met the deadline.” Meanwhile, the federal court case continues through court filings. People Not Politicians elevated their appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court, asking Judge Brett Kavanaugh to respond by 9 a.m. Missouri-time Thursday. Hoskins is facing off against People Not Politicians, the citizen activist group that successfully fought to strike down the Republican-favored map in state court. Their attorney, Chuck Hatfield, strongly rejects the argument that federal law overrides the state supreme court’s authority in this instance. “This issue is a matter of state law, there are what we call in the business, independent state grounds for this decision, it is not a matter of federal law,” Hatfield said. In a newly submitted suggestions filing, Hatfield urged the state supreme court to hold Hoskins in civil contempt. Hatfield argued that Hoskins’ team actively ginned up the “friendly” federal lawsuit to manufacture a conflict and bypass the state’s highest authority. In filings, Hatfield suggested the court bypass Hoskins entirely by directly ordering local election authorities not to use the HB 1 map. Legal experts and political analysts agree that the clash between state and federal jurisdictions is an extraordinary and rare scenario. Former Missouri Supreme Court Justice Mike Wolff likened the situation to one of the most famous election disputes in U.S. history. “It really feels like Bush versus Gore,” Wolff said. “’Cause in that case, Florida courts were adjudicating the count of votes in Florida, and the U.S. Supreme Court stepped in and said, ‘Oh wait a minute, there’s gonna be an equal protection problem here.’” However, Wolff emphasized that because state laws generally govern elections, Hoskins remains legally answerable to the state court system. “I think the question for Hoskins is, do you have an obligation to obey the orders of the Supreme Court of Missouri? And the answer to that is a resounding yes,” Wolff said. As for what happens next at tomorrow’s hearing, Wolff admitted, “Especially in this situation, who knows?” Nathan Carrington, PhD, a political scientist at Saint Louis University, agrees that the issue will likely land on the steps of the nation’s highest court. “Who knows where this is going to end up. I do think this is going to go back to the Supreme Court in some way, I don’t think they’re gonna be able to dodge it the way they did before,” Carrington said. With the high-stakes hearing scheduled for Thursday, time is rapidly running out for local election officials. Local clerks are hoping for immediate clarity. They are currently working against a tight deadline to prepare and mail out November absentee ballots starting next week. “Time is of the essence and the courts are aware of that, so whatever is going to happen is probably going to happen pretty quick in the next few days,” Carrington noted. Dr Olav Fykse Tveit, Church of Norway presiding bishop, offered a sermon with a message of hope: love never ends. “Most things come to an end in this life. Almost everything. But not love,” said Tveit. “Life and love are the greatest gifts God has given us. And the greatest of these is love, stronger even than death itself.” Tveit noted that the love between the people and King Harald has not come to an end. “Quite the contrary. The sea of flowers, with all the words and drawings placed among them, speaks with a strong and clear voice of what fills our hearts to overflowing. Love has become tears of grief,” Tveit said. “We also know that love can appear to have its limits.” Death separates us from one another, Tveit lamented. “Such is our human condition,” he said. “Nor do we always succeed in loving our neighbour as ourselves, even though we try and sincerely desire to do so.” We see even many signs in our world that love does not always prevail, reflected Tveit. “Yet love does not end,” he said. “It remains before us as a calling, as a vision, as an ideal towards which we may all stretch ourselves.” King Harald, who died on 28 August at age 89, was Europe’s oldest monarch and had reigned for 35 years. Ahead of the funeral, more than 46,000 people visited Harald’s coffin as it laid in state in the chapel of the royal palace. title: State of Oregon v. Trump - Cato Institute
content: The Federal Circuit should affirm the decision of the Court of International Trade and declare the new round of tariffs to be illegal. Learn more about Cato’s Amicus Briefs Program. In February 2026, the Supreme Court invalidated the massive tariffs that President Trump attempted to impose under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA). But that decision did not end Trump’s efforts to unilaterally impose onerous tariffs. Now the President has invoked Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 to purportedly impose 10 percent tariffs on imports from almost all US trading partners. Soon after these new tariffs were announced, two small businesses and a coalition of 24 state governments filed lawsuits in the US Court of International Trade (CIT) challenging their legality. In May, the CIT ruled that these new tariffs are illegal. Now the case has been appealed to the US Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit. Cato and Professor Ilya Somin, our B. Kenneth Simon Chair in Constitutional Studies, have filed an amicus brief supporting the CIT’s decision; Somin previously served as co-counsel to the victorious plaintiffs in the IEEPA Supreme Court tariff case. We thank Daniel Wolff, Alexander Schaefer, and Joshua Claybourn of Crowell & Moring for assistance in drafting and filing the brief. In our brief, we explain why this sweeping imposition of tariffs is just as illegal as the previous one was, and for many of the same reasons. First, our brief explains why Section 122 simply cannot be used in the current circumstances. The statute only permits tariffs for up to 150 days in response to “fundamental international payments problems” that cause “large and serious United States balance-of-payments deficits” or “an imminent and significant depreciation of the dollar,” or that create a need to cooperate with other countries in addressing an “international balance-of-payments disequilibrium.” But these conditions are only possible under a fixed exchange rate system, such as the one the US formerly had under the gold standard. These conditions cannot and do not exist in a flexible exchange rate regime of the sort in place today. Next, we explain why, if there is any ambiguity about whether Section 122 authorizes the massive tariffs imposed by the administration, the major questions doctrine requires this issue to be resolved against the government. The major questions doctrine requires Congress to “speak clearly” when it assigns to the executive “decisions of vast economic and political significance.” The impact of the new Section 122 tariffs is as large or larger than many previous policies invalidated by the Supreme Court on major questions doctrine grounds. And the tariff power is not exempt from major questions scrutiny on the supposed ground that it is a “foreign affairs” power. The major questions doctrine also counts against giving the administration a blank check in determining whether the preconditions to invoke Section 122 exist. Finally, if the court were to conclude that Section 122 does somehow grant the president the sweeping power he claims, it must rule that the law is an unconstitutional delegation of legislative power to the executive. Congress cannot give the president what would essentially be unlimited power to impose up to 15% tariffs on imports from any nation, especially since the administration’s approach would allow the executive to circumvent the 150-day time limit simply by declaring that a new balance-of-payments crisis has arisen after it expires. The Federal Circuit should affirm the decision of the Court of International Trade and declare the new round of tariffs to be illegal. Professor of Law, George Mason University, and B. Kenneth Simon Chair in Constitutional Studies, Cato Institute Director, Robert A. Levy Center for Constitutional Studies, Cato Institute Every weekday morning: independent analysis grounded in individual liberty, limited government, free markets, and peace.

title: LIVE: King Harald V’s funeral: Royal families from around the world gather in Oslo to say goodbye [Updating] - HOLA
content: Today, Wednesday, September 9th, the eyes of the world are on Oslo for the State Funeral of King Harald V of Norway, who passed away on August 28 at the age of 89 after several days in the hospital. Since then, the entire country has been mourning the loss of its beloved sovereign, regarded by several generations as the “grandfather of the nation.” Since Tuesday afternoon, numerous royals have arrived, among them King Felipe and Queen Letizia; Princess Alexia of Greece with her husband, Carlos Morlaes, her brother, Prince Nikolaos of Greece, and her mother, Queen Anne-Marie; Alois of Liechtenstein; Abdullah and Rania of Jordan; and Rosario Nadal, a close friend of Queen Mette-Marit. They were all seen around the Grand Hotel as they gathered for a historic reception hosted by Haakon VIII and Mette-Marit. King Harald’s coffin has arrived at Akershus Fortress, his final resting place. Located in the heart of Oslo overlooking the fjord, Akershus is one of Norway’s most important historic landmarks. Construction began around 1290, and over the centuries it evolved from a medieval castle into a fortress. For more than 700 years, Akershus has been closely tied to Norway’s monarchy and government, and today it is home to the royal mausoleum. Following King Harald’s funeral service, Crown Princess Victoria of Sweden and Princess Catharina-Amalia of the Netherlands were seen sharing a relaxed conversation. Both are future queens, although they belong to different generations of European royalty. One of the most poignant images of the day was King Haakon of Norway surrounded by King Carl XVI Gustaf of Sweden and King Frederik X of Denmark during the final procession before King Harald’s burial. The three Scandinavian monarchies share deep historical ties and decades of friendship. In a final tribute, Norwegian Armed Forces aircraft flew over Oslo before King Harald V’s coffin began its journey to his final resting place in the crypt at Akershus Castle. The procession continued to the sound of a funeral march performed by a military band. Following the funeral, King Harald’s coffin is being carried in procession to Akershus Castle Church, where a private ceremony will be held for the family and royal guests. The president of the Storting, Norway’s prime minister and the chief justice of the Supreme Court will also attend, along with the presidents of Iceland and Finland. The coffin will then be lowered into the crypt of the castle church, where King Haakon VII, Queen Maud, King Olav V and Crown Princess Märtha are also laid to rest. “We give thanks for King Harald and for all you have given us through his life” “Eternal God, our refuge in this time of sorrow, draw near to us with your peace. Strengthen us in faith. Give us a future and hope. We give thanks for King Harald and for all you have given us through his life. Merciful God, we commend him into your hands. You who created us in your image and gave us Jesus Christ as our Savior, raise us on the last day to eternal life with you,” the farewell prayer read. In one of the more emotional moments of the service, Princess Ingrid Alexandra offered support to her younger brother, Prince Sverre Magnus, during the performance of Abide with Me. “May the Lord bless you and keep you; may the Lord make his face shine upon you and be gracious to you; may the Lord turn his face toward you and give you peace.” Crown Princess Victoria of Sweden stepped forward to lead a prayer, first making a final curtsy to her godfather, King Harald. The future queen of Sweden then read the Prayer of St. Francis in Swedish. The prayer carries special significance for Victoria and the Norwegian royal family. She recited the same prayer when King Haakon and Queen Mette-Marit married at Oslo Cathedral in 2001. The Swedish crown princess was also among the first royals to support the relationship of Norway’s now King and Queen. Music has played a central role throughout King Harald’s funeral, accompanying some of the most moving moments of the historic service. The ceremony was presided over by Presiding Bishop Olav Fykse Tveit and followed the funeral rites of the Church of Norway. Bishop of Oslo Sunniva Gylver also took part in the service. A passage from the Gospel of John was read in Sámi during the funeral service: “I am the good shepherd. I know my own and my own know me. I give them eternal life, and they will never perish. No one will take them out of my hand. What my Father has given me is greater than all else, and no one can take it out of the Father’s hand.” Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre also paid tribute to Queen Sonja, highlighting her tireless dedication to culture, nature and traveling to even the most remote corners of Norway. “I have an image etched in my memory. At the top of Stortinden, in Vågan municipality in Lofoten, stands Dronningvarden, with the words ‘for a country.’ But I say, on behalf of all of us, for a queen.” The traditional song “Jørgen Hattemaker” was performed during the funeral service. The song tells the story of a hatmaker who compares his life with that of King Solomon. Despite the differences between them, both ultimately share the same fundamental condition as human beings. “We are deeply grateful for King Harald’s 35 years as King of Norway, but above all for the person he was. He brought humanity to the solemnity of the monarchy. When we were happy, he was happy with us, with laughter and a twinkle in his eye,” Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said. The President of the Norwegian Parliament delivers the first address during King Harald’s funeral service at Oslo Cathedral. The entire nation observes a minute of silence in honor of King Harald, beginning and ending with three tolls of the bell. The guests inside Oslo Cathedral then take their seats. All guests have now taken their seats inside Oslo Cathedral as King Harald’s funeral service begins. The King’s family is seated on one side of the altar, while members of royal families from around the world are seated on the other. A Royal Guard soldier fainted at Palace Square shortly before King Harald’s funeral procession began. The soldier lost consciousness and has since been evacuated. According to Norwegian news agency NTB, another soldier was also removed from formation at a different location. More than 200,000 people, including 53,000 in central Oslo, have taken part in King Harald’s state funeral, as Norway comes together for a historic and deeply solemn royal farewell. Upon their arrival at Oslo Cathedral, Queen Sonja, King Haakon and Queen Mette-Marit, Princess Märtha Louise, Princess Ingrid Alexandra and Prince Sverre Magnus were welcomed by church officials. Other members of the royal families in attendance then began entering the cathedral. Princess Märtha Louise’s three daughters, Maud Angelica, Leah Isadora and Emma Tallulah, have entered Oslo Cathedral alongside Durek Verrett and Marius Borg Høiby. King Harald’s funeral procession is approaching Oslo Cathedral as thousands of Norwegians line the streets, respectfully paying their final tribute to the late monarch. A profound silence has fallen over Oslo as King Harald’s funeral procession makes its way through the city. Alongside the Norwegian royal family, members of royal families from across Europe have joined this solemn moment, including King Felipe and Queen Letizia of Spain, King Willem-Alexander and Queen Máxima of the Netherlands, and their daughter, Princess Catharina-Amalia. King Haakon, accompanied by his children, Princess Ingrid Alexandra and Prince Sverre Magnus, and his sister, Princess Märtha Louise, escorts King Harald’s coffin during his final journey through the crowded streets of Oslo. Queens Mette-Marit and Sonja follow in a car behind them. King Harald’s coffin has left the chapel at the Royal Palace, where members of his family and dozens of Norwegians paid their respects, and is now making its way to Oslo Cathedral for the funeral service. Draped in the royal standard and topped with a wreath of flowers, the coffin has been placed on a purple velvet catafalque. Prince Albert and Princess Charlene of Monaco were seen boarding the bus that will take them to Oslo Cathedral for King Harald V’s state funeral. The Grimaldi flag is also flying at half-staff in Monaco as a sign of mourning following the Norwegian monarch’s death. Queen Rania of Jordan was also seen leaving the Grand Hotel in the Norwegian capital, following the royal protocol and dress code for the solemn occasion. Grand Duchess Maria Teresa shared a heartfelt tribute ahead of the funeral: “On this day of the funeral of the much-loved King of Norway, I remember with emotion the immense affection he always showed me. I will never forget his wonderful sense of humor either.” Dressed in military uniform, King Frederik X left the Danish royal yacht alongside his wife, Queen Mary, as the couple made their way to King Harald’s funeral. The Danish royals chose to travel to Oslo aboard their own vessel and spend the night there rather than stay at a hotel. Marius Borg Høiby, who is serving a four-year sentence from Skaugum Palace, was seen leaving by car as part of a motorcade that also included his mother, Queen Mette-Marit, King Haakon VIII, Princess Ingrid Alexandra and Prince Sverre Magnus. As Harald V’s coffin is carried through the streets of Oslo to his final resting place, every branch of the Armed Forces will be represented to render him their last honors. A total of 1,900 service members from all the services will line the route along the streets. The United Kingdom, Sweden, and Denmark have also sent troops. In addition to being closed to traffic, downtown Oslo has been equipped with giant screens so people can follow all of today’s events. More than 170 churches across the country will also broadcast the funeral ceremony live. King Philippe and Queen Mathilde of Belgium and the Grand Duke and Grand Duchess of Luxembourg, Guillaume and Stéphanie, have arrived together by bus. The monarchs are dressed in their full ceremonial uniforms and decorations. The Swedish Royal Family has already landed in Oslo. It is one of the monarchies sending the largest delegation to this State Funeral, due to strong family and friendship ties. Crown Princess Victoria is one of King Harald’s godchildren and one of those who has most deeply mourned the loss of her “dear” godfather. In addition, King Carl Gustaf has already announced that on Wednesday there will be a bell-ringing ceremony at Riddarholm Church in Stockholm. Harald V was appointed Knight of the Royal Order of the Seraphim by King Gustaf VI Adolf in 1958. In 1992, he received the chain of this Order. Before 9:00 a.m., King Felipe VI’s standard was lowered to half-mast at the Royal Palace in Madrid as a sign of mourning on the day of King Harald V of Norway’s funeral. At the moment of his interment, it will be raised to the top of the mast in tribute to King Haakon VIII. Despite his recent kidney transplant, Durek Verrett arrived at the Royal Palace with his wife, Princess Märtha Louise of Norway, to join the Norwegian Royal Family in their grief and in this major tribute to King Harald. Princess Märtha Louise is no longer an active member of the Royal Family, but she always maintained a very close and loving relationship with her father. King Harald and Queen Sonja attended their daughter’s wedding to the shaman to the Hollywood stars. Very early on Wednesday morning, at 7:00 a.m., Queen Sonja was seen out for a walk in sportswear through the Royal Palace park. Cell phone in hand, she took a photo of her own statue, which was covered in flowers. Today will be an incredibly difficult day for her: she will say a final goodbye to the man she was married to for almost 58 years and with whom she shared a royal love story unlike any other. Oslo has gone into maximum security mode for an event that has posed a major security and logistical challenge. Flights have been canceled at the airport so that planes carrying royals and dignitaries from around the world can land to say farewell to the Nordic monarch. © ¡HOLA! People are not happy about Flock Safety’s automated license plate readers and the cops that allegedly misuse them. If you’re one of those ALPR-haters, you can now take out your rage in the video game Grand Theft Auto V by installing Grand Theft Automated License Plate Reader, a mod built by artist Morry Kolman. The mod installs 235 Flock cameras around the fictional Los Santos, a riff on the real-life city of Los Angeles. Players can smash and shoot down the cameras and get paid $600 for each one they destroy, which Kolman priced based on a teardown of a Flock Falcon Flex Camera by the Iowa-based civil liberties group Eyes Off of Cedar Rapids. The in-game cameras log every time a player destroys and drives by one, and players can render a photo album of their interactions. In real life, vigilantes have allegedly wrecked Flock cameras in their communities using spray-paint, saws, bullets, and even flaming projectiles. An NPR analysis found that Flock cameras have been vandalized in at least 36 states. “GTPLR is not an endorsement of the activities that it allows in the game in the same way that GTA is not an endorsement of the activities that are allowed in the game,” says Kolman, referring to the fact that GTA is largely about doing fictional crimes. “But I think there is a public appetite for some kind of cathartic release against these machines.” In addition to being fun objects to destroy, the GTA cameras also operate as an extension of the police in-game. Passing by one of the 235 cameras while being chased by the cops prolongs the game’s cooldown period. Because of how dense the cameras are in some areas, it can make the game impossible to play. There’s also a 5 percent chance that the cameras will trigger a random police response even if the player isn’t doing anything wrong, which Kolman says was inspired by news reports about innocent people being held at gunpoint because of ALPR errors. “There are violent responses and really dangerous situations that are created by these cameras and their inaccuracies,” says Kolman. Flock did not immediately respond to a request for comment for this story. GTA V has been around for over a decade, and a rich modding community has built up around it (WIRED covered one back in 2015.) The long-awaited sequel, Grand Theft Auto VI, is slated to come out in November and will be set in a fictional version of Miami called Vice City. Kolman doesn’t have specific plans to build a version of GTALPR for that, joking, “We'll probably wait to see what the people of Vice City and their local government have already installed around their map.” In real-life LA, the Los Angeles Police Department suspended its use of Flock cameras this summer following a recommendation from the LAPD’s inspector general. The tide is turning in other places too—governors in both Texas and Florida recently took steps to curtail the use of Flock cameras in their respective states, and across the US, there were 131 Flock contract terminations in August alone, according to the anti-surveillance advocacy group Secure Justice. For all the fun that fake-smashing surveillance cameras can be, Kolman seriously hopes that players can feel the “insidiousness and inescapability of the surveillance” through GTALPR. “I know that you could read a thousand articles about why surveillance is bad and why Flock is horrible,” says Kolman. “Or I could make you feel how pervasive these Flock cameras are by having you try to drive around the map of Los Santos.” Be the first to start the conversation! title: An Elegant Royal Farewell to King Harald V of Norway in Oslo - The Court Jeweller
content: Don’t Miss a Single Sparkling Moment! Sign up for The Court Jeweller Newsletter The extended royal family gathered in the Norwegian capital today to bid farewell to King Harald V of Norway in a state funeral service held at Oslo Cathedral. King Haakon VIII of Norway led the mourners today at the funeral for his late father, King Harald V, in Oslo. The late monarch’s coffin was transported from the Royal Palace to Oslo Cathedral in a solemn procession. King Haakon VIII, Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra, Prince Sverre Magnus, and Princess Märtha Louise walked behind the coffin. In a remarkable sight for the modern era, the procession also included numerous other royals, including the sovereigns of Sweden, Denmark, Belgium, the Netherlands, Jordan, Spain, Luxembourg, and Monaco, and the heirs of the United Kingdom, Japan, and Liechtenstein. Nearly all of the royal ladies in attendance wore the expected mourning attire: black with pearls. Here, Queen Sonja of Norway arrives with her son, King Haakon VIII, for the service. She also pinned her late husband’s Royal Family Order to her dress. Queen Mette-Marit also wore the late King’s Royal Family Order, plus pearl and diamond cluster earrings and a three-row pearl necklace. Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra wore King Harald’s Royal Family Order with a special necklace. The heart-shaped pendant, suspended from a single row of pearls, is set with diamonds and a central ruby, reflecting Norway’s national colors. The necklace was given to Ingrid Alexandra by her grandmother, Queen Sonja, as a christening present in 2004. Princess Märtha Louise arrived for her father’s funeral wearing his Royal Family Order and pearls, including a lovely five-row choker necklace with an antique diamond and pearl clasp. King Harald’s sister, Princess Astrid, wore pearls as well, plus the Royal Family Orders of her brother, their father (King Olav V), and their grandfather (King Haakon VII). The deep family and diplomatic ties between the late King and heads of state around the world were reflected in the guest list for the funeral. The entire Swedish royal family was in attendance: King Carl XVI Gustaf and Queen Silvia (who wore pearls with an antique diamond bow brooch), Crown Princess Victoria and Prince Daniel, Prince Carl Philip and Princess Sofia, Princess Madeleine and Chris O’Neill, and Princess Christina and Tord Magnuson. King Harald was Crown Princess Victoria’s godfather, and she read a prayer during the funeral service. She wore pearl earrings, a pearl necklace with a cluster clasp, and a lovely antique heart-shaped mourning brooch. Sarah Williams has confirmed that the brooch was a gift to Victoria from King Harald. Princess Sofia and Princess Madeleine wore minimal jewelry: a little cluster brooch on Sofia’s coat, and small stud earrings for Madeleine. Denmark was represented by King Frederik X, Queen Mary, and Crown Prince Christian, plus Princess Benedikte with Princess Alexandra of Sayn-Wittgenstein-Berleburg. (Queen Margrethe was scheduled to attend but had to cancel following a recent hospitalization.) Mary wore pearl and diamond earrings and a pearl and diamond cluster brooch from a suite of jewels that belonged to Queen Lovisa of Denmark, King Harald’s great-grandmother. The Greek royal branch of the Danish royal family was also well-represented, with Queen Anne-Marie, Crown Prince Pavlos, Prince Nikolaos, Princess Alexia, and Carlos Morales Quintana also in attendance at the service. Queen Anne-Marie wore a golden flower brooch for the occasion. The Belgian royals and Norwegian royals are close cousins—King Harald’s mother, Crown Princess Märtha, and King Philippe’s grandmother, Queen Astrid, were sisters. For the funeral, Queen Mathilde wore a pearl choker, her diamond butterfly brooch, and Queen Fabiola’s pearl drop earrings. She wore the same combination of jewels for the funeral of Queen Elizabeth II four years ago. The Luxembourgish royals are also close cousins, as Grand Duke Guillaume V is a great-grandson of Queen Astrid. He attended alongside his wife, Grand Duchess Stéphanie, who wore earrings set with dark gemstones, and his father, Grand Duke Henri. The Dutch royal family was represented by King Willem-Alexander, Queen Máxima, Princess Amalia, and Princess Beatrix. Máxima wore pearl earrings with a nineteenth-century pearl and diamond brooch from the family collection. Máxima also wore this brooch for Queen Elizabeth II’s state funeral in 2022. Princess Amalia borrowed pearl and diamond earrings from her mother’s collection for the occasion. She also wore a pearl ring. Amalia sat beside her grandmother, Princess Beatrix, during the service. Beatrix wore more pearl jewelry, including a bangle bracelet with pearl tips. Queen Letizia of Spain wore her Ansorena diamond and pearl drop earrings for the service, plus a special necklace. The strand of pearls is part of Queen Ena’s joyas de pasar collection, which is earmarked for the use of the Queen of Spain. Queen Sofia wore pearls, too, though photos of her weren’t plentiful. Here, you catch a glimpse of her as she greets the Prince of Wales, the grandson of her Greek royal cousin, Prince Philip. The King and Queen of Jordan were present as well. Queen Rania does not usually wear much traditional jewelry for these kinds of mourning events, and today was no exception. Also in minimal jewelry—pearl stud earrings and her diamond engagement ring—was Princess Charlene of Monaco, who attended with her husband, Prince Albert II. Hereditary Princess Sophie of Liechtenstein brought along pearl and diamond pieces for the service, including a two-row pearl necklace and a lovely diamond ribbon brooch. We saw her wear the same brooch at Queen Elizabeth II’s funeral in 2022. The Emperor and Empress of Japan were represented by Crown Prince Fumihito and Crown Princess Kiko, who wore black earrings and a matching beaded necklace, plus a luminous dark bow brooch. Prince William represented his father at the funeral, but there was also another British royal family member in attendance: the Princess Royal, who wore her gold and diamond ribbon brooch for the service. Anne was present in a personal capacity; she is King Haakon’s godmother. The former monarchy of Serbia was represented by Crown Prince Alexander, who has remained close to his Scandinavian cousins over the years. He was joined by Crown Princess Katherine, who wore a gold ring on her right hand. After the funeral, the King’s body was interred in the Royal Mausoleum at Akershus Castle, beside his parents and his grandparents. The royals returned to the Royal Palace, where they held an official reception for their guests. King Haakon VIII, Queen Mette-Marit, Queen Sonja, Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra, and Prince Sverre Magnus also made a brief appearance on the palace balcony, waving in gratitude to the thousands of mourners gathered below. This story is taken from the autumn 2026 issue of Dazed, which is on sale internationally from September 10. Pre-order a copy of the magazine here. Everywhere V goes, he is accompanied by screams. Whether he’s attending a fashion show, performing at a sold-out arena or even making the short trip from his blacked-out SUV to the foyer of a five-star hotel, the BTS star’s life is soundtracked by an unbroken chorus of ear-splitting shrieks. When I meet him away from the crowds, in a nondescript studio in central Paris, the contrast between this mania and his calm, gentle demeanour is stark. In person, V is softly spoken, flawlessly polite and has a cheeky, slightly goofy sense of humour. Together, these qualities make for an endearing combination. Excluding the photoshoot, we are granted just two short audiences with him; both conversations are strictly off the record. (Although I can confirm that he essentially just introduced himself, asked if I’d been to Korea, said he could recommend some restaurants for the next time I was in Seoul, and thanked us for having him on the cover of the magazine.) The scale of V’s success, along with his bandmates j-hope, Jimin, Jin, Jung Kook, RM and Suga, is difficult to comprehend. In 2024, BTS became the most-streamed band of all time on Spotify, becoming the first to surpass 100bn streams across all platforms with the release of their tenth album, ARIRANG, in March this year. Along with the Beatles, they are one of only two groups in history to score three number one albums on the US Billboard chart in a single year. In fact, in terms of cultural impact, the Beatles are the only band that offers a meaningful comparison. One in 13 tourists to South Korea cites BTS as their main reason for visiting, and the group contributes an estimated US$4.65bn to the Korean economy each year. V is the soulful “fashion diva” (his stylist’s words) of the group, known for his rich baritone voice and retro, romantic style (see: his preference for louche tailoring and Michael Rider’s Celine). He reached a million followers on Instagram within 43 minutes of opening his account in 2021 – a Guinness World Record feat – and is now, with 75 million fans and counting, the most followed male K-pop artist on the platform. This is all to say that V is one of the most formidable forces in contemporary pop. But what do we know about the man himself? Well, at the age of 30, he’s recently completed 18 months of active service in the South Korean army, serving in an elite counter-terrorism unit under the military police. He was born on December 30, 1995, in Daegu, the fourth-largest city in South Korea, and was raised largely by his paternal grandparents while his parents worked. He debuted with BTS when he was just 17, after accompanying a friend to an audition where he was spotted by recruiters. After more than a decade with the band, he launched his solo career with his debut EP, Layover, in September 2023. He’s a Capricorn sun, an Aries moon and (according to BTS fan sites) a Sagittarius rising. He loves animals and had a black-and-tan pomeranian called Yeontan, who sadly died in 2024. He likes jazz, photography, art and fashion; Bing Crosby, Louis Armstrong, Kurt Cobain and John Legend. And despite channelling some of these musicians into his cool-guy-in-a-smoky-club aesthetic, he doesn’t take himself too seriously – as evidenced by his unfiltered chats with fans on Weverse, the general buffoonery of Run BTS, and his willingness to eat a series of increasingly spicy chicken wings on YouTube. The stage feels like V’s natural habitat. He performs with such ease, such deftness, that it’s clear this is what he was born – and trained – to do. At a London stop in the group’s ongoing world tour, he could be seen gliding around the stage, floating from flawless vocals to faultless choreography, barely breaking a sweat despite the sweltering July heat. Seeing him perform prompts a million questions. How is he doing? Does he enjoy this life? What’s it like being screamed at all the time? Is he happy? Does he have friends outside the band? When does he hang out with them? What do they get up to? What occupies his mind when no one is watching? What does the explore page on his Finsta look like? What was his time in the military like? Did he enjoy it? Is he still in touch with anyone from his unit? What is it like to be recognised by so many but known by so few? The tight-lipped nature of the K-pop industry means that a lot of these questions won’t be answered – at least not here. But what follows is our attempt to get to know this idol, who stands at the very pinnacle of global pop culture. Hi V. How would you describe this current chapter of your life? V: We’ve been really busy [lately] with our BTS WORLD TOUR ARIRANG in Europe, and I’ve had the chance to experience so many different cities along the way. Every place feels unfamiliar at first, but I’ve been finding small moments of happiness that feel comforting and make me feel at home. Your life has been very busy for a long time. What helps you feel grounded? V: What helps me stay grounded when everything moves so quickly is learning to appreciate the present moment. I’m trying to focus on the fact that I can have a good day without always having to rush or achieve something. I’ve realised that, even during a busy life, it’s important to slow down and enjoy where I am right now. I feel most like myself on stage, when I’m able to express who I am through performance V: Right now, while I’m on tour with BTS, what helps me reconnect with myself the most is being on stage. That’s the moment I feel the most like myself, when I can fully express who I am through performance. Another important part is our fans, ARMY. They remind me why I chose this path and help me remember the passion that started my journey in the first place. What do you think you would be doing if you weren’t a musician? V: I’ve thought about it before, but whenever I do it feels a little scary, so I just tell myself to stop overthinking. It reminds me how grateful I am to be making music. I’m happy with the life I have now, so I just try to enjoy each moment and do my best. You were 17 when you debuted with BTS. What advice would you give to your younger self? V: If I could give my younger self one piece of advice, I would tell him to stay focused on music. There may be moments when he becomes curious about things beyond music, and exploring new experiences is important, but I would remind him to always remember why he started this journey and continue to put his heart into music. Has your definition of success changed since you first debuted? V: When I first debuted, I think I had a very simple definition of success. I thought that, if I could appear on TV, that meant I had succeeded. But now I see success a little differently. Being able to share my music and my story with people is still meaningful, but I also think success is about being able to continue doing what I love and being remembered in a positive way. What is the best piece of advice you’ve been given? And who was it that gave it to you? V: One piece of advice that has stayed with me is, ‘You’ve done well, you’re doing well, and things will work out, so get some good rest’. It was something a close older friend told me a long time ago, during a moment when I was lacking confidence and needed some encouragement. I still remember those words, because they gave me comfort when I needed it most. Sometimes, even after all these years, that simple message comes back to me and reminds me to keep going. What was turning 30 like for you? Has your mentality changed since hitting this age? V: Honestly, I don’t think there was a big difference when I entered my 30s. Other than realising I need a little more time to recover than I used to, I don’t feel like much has changed. I’m still the same person, with the same passion and mindset. You’ve often spoken about how important your grandmother was in your life. Is there a particular memory of her that still stays with you today? V: My grandmother is someone who means so much to me. When I was growing up, she always made delicious meals for me, so I don’t really remember having many experiences of eating out until I was in elementary school. I think the first time I had a meal outside was probably my elementary school graduation day. I still remember how special that moment felt, and how much I enjoyed her meals. Looking back, those moments with my grandmother were filled with so much love and care, and they are memories I still cherish today. How would you describe the new BTS album? How would you like it to make people feel? V: ARIRANG is about BTS’s identity and our roots. I believe this album shows our growth and who we have become over the years. During the making of the album, our different personalities and perspectives came together, and I think those differences are what made the music more colourful and honest. Ultimately, we hope ARIRANG becomes a timeless piece of work that can resonate with people across generations and cultures. When I first debuted, I had a very simple definition of success. But now I see [things] differently How would you define your role in the group, musically and also in terms of personality? V: I think of myself as someone who helps to balance the energy within the group. If the mood gets too high, I will try to bring it down and create a sense of calm, and if things feel a little too quiet, I’ll try to lift the vibe. I feel like I help create the right balance. V: I feel the most confident right after a performance. When I walk back into my hotel room after a show, I’m usually filled with so much energy and confidence because I’m still carrying the excitement from the stage. I come back to my hotel, take a shower and get ready to sleep feeling really content and proud, but because the adrenaline is still there it’s not always easy to fall asleep right away. What’s one thing people often assume about you that isn’t quite true? V: I’m a pretty honest person, so I’m not sure if there’s anything people often misunderstand about me. But if there’s something people are curious about or want to know, I’d be happy for them to ask. What are you curious about at the moment? Is there something you’re trying to learn or understand that has nothing to do with your music? V: These days, I’ve been really into learning the piano. It’s something I’ve been enjoying and exploring at my own pace. If we’re talking about something completely unrelated to music, I would say travel. I’m looking forward to a quiet kind of travel where I can slow down, take in new surroundings and have time to enjoy the moment. When people look back on your career many years from now, what do you hope they remember – not just about your work, but about you as a person? V: I hope people remember me as an artist who could express a wide spectrum of emotions. I want my work to reflect different feelings and stories, and I hope those emotions can reach people in their own way. title: Norway's King Harald V laid to rest in state funeral - DW.com
content: Heads of state from around the world came to Oslo to pay tribute to the late monarch. A 21-gun salute rang out over Oslo on Wednesday afternoon as the coffin of Norway's King Harald V left the royal palace for the city's Lutheran cathedral. Thousands of people lined the streets to say goodbye to the king. Norway then observed a minute of silence to start the funeral service. The procession and funeral brought an end to 13 days of national mourning following the death of the well-liked  monarch at the age of 89. "He struck a balance between being stately and being down-to-earth," Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store said in his eulogy. "He made Norway greater. He spoke of a 'we' in Norway where everyone is there for each other." After the ceremony, his casket was moved to its final resting place at the royal palace chapel. A private ceremony just for family followed. The funeral was attended by heads of state and government from all over the world. They included the UK's Prince William and Princess Anne, Japan's Crown Prince Fumihito and his wife Princess Kiko, Spain's King Felipe and Queen Letizia, as well as fellow Scandinavian royals from Denmark and Sweden. Other leaders such as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Germany's President Frank-Walter Steinmeier were also attending. Indeed, flags were flown at half-mast in Berlin's government in honor of Harald, whose 35-year-reign made him well-known and respected across Europe. Harald's son King Haakon VIII was be there alongside his family including his mother Queen Sonja and his wife, Queen Mette-Marit. Controversially, Mette-Marit's son from a previous relationship was also expected to be at the funeral. Marius Borg Hoiby's participation in an earlier part of the official mourning drew an outcry in Norway, as he was recently convicted of rape and domestic violence and is under house arrest. title: Norway bids final farewell to popular King Harald V as crowds and royals converge for his funeral - abcnews.com
content: Norway has bid its final farewell to Harald V as crowds line the streets and foreign royals and leaders converge on Oslo for the funeral of the long-serving king OSLO, Norway -- Norway bade its final farewell to Harald V on Wednesday as crowds lined the streets and foreign royals and leaders converged on Oslo for the funeral of the long-serving king, who was remembered as a popular monarch with a down-to-earth touch. A 21-gun salute rang out over the capital at the start of a funeral procession from the royal palace to Oslo Cathedral. Harald’s son, new King Haakon VIII, and other senior royals walked behind the coffin, draped with the red Norwegian royal standard. Harald’s widow, Queen Sonja, and Haakon’s wife, Queen Mette-Marit, followed in a car. Norwegian officials and foreign dignitaries joined the solemn procession. They included the monarchs of Sweden, Denmark, Spain, the Netherlands, Belgium, Luxembourg, Monaco and Jordan. Also present were the heir to the British throne, Prince William, and Japan’s Crown Prince Akishino, as well as political leaders from more than 20 countries, including Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. As the funeral service began, Norway came to a halt for a minute of silence. Harald, who died on Aug. 28 aged 89, was Europe’s oldest monarch and had reigned for 35 years. He modernized the royal house but refused to follow in the footsteps of other aging monarchs who recently abdicated. His son immediately became king and last week took an oath of allegiance to Norway’s constitution in parliament. The parliament's speaker, Masud Gharahkhani, said at the service that “King Harald was close to the people” and recalled that “he wasn’t afraid to meet people in his rubber boots.” He remembered Harald saying in his 2008 New Year's address: “I wish we would stop using the term ‘the weakest in society.’ In reality, some of these people are among the strongest of us all.” “He lived up to his motto: He gave his all for Norway,” Gharahkhani said. Large crowds flocked to Oslo for the funeral, and thousands stood behind barriers on streets lined with national flags. The downtown area was closed to vehicles and electric scooters, and police had instructed people not to bring bicycles, umbrellas or sharp objects. People tuned in across the country of about 5.6 million. Scores of churches, libraries, cultural centers and city halls made big screens available for the public to watch the funeral, public broadcaster NRK reported. The government said it wasn’t an official holiday, but schools and workplaces could individually opt to let students and employees watch. Ahead of the funeral, Norwegians waited patiently to file past Harald's coffin in the chapel of the royal palace. The queue was seven hours long at one point over the weekend. Over 46,000 people visited the chapel during the week it lay in state. “The love between the people and King Harald has not ended — quite the contrary,” said Bishop Olav Fykse Tveit, who led the funeral service, pointing to the tributes left outside the palace after his death. “The sea of flowers, along with the words and drawings that accompany them, speaks loudly and clearly of a heart so full that it overflows.” After the funeral, Harald's coffin was taken in a smaller procession to Akershus Fortress, where his predecessors are buried in the crypt of the palace chapel. Haakon followed with the two other Scandinavian monarchs, King Carl XVI Gustaf of Sweden and King Frederik X of Denmark. Among those who attended the funeral was Mette-Marit’s eldest son and Haakon's stepson, Marius Borg Høiby, who has no royal title or duties. Høiby is appealing against a rape conviction after a trial earlier this year that cast a shadow over the royal family. Norway’s monarchy traces its origins to King Harald Fairhair in the ninth century. When Norway regained its independence from Sweden in 1905, three-quarters of voters in a national plebiscite approved restoring the monarchy. The Norwegian royal house has kinfolk in other European royal families. Harald and Haakon are related to both Britain’s King Charles III and Spain’s King Felipe VI: They’re all descendants of the U.K.'s Queen Victoria, who reigned from 1837 until her death in 1901. Today, the throne's role is largely symbolic and power lies with the elected government and parliament, but the Norwegian royal family retains a role in promoting the wealthy Scandinavian nation around the world. Associated Press writers Geir Moulson in Berlin, Jamey Keaten in Geneva and Claudia Ciobanu in Warsaw, Poland contributed to this report. title: Sněť – “V bažinách vědomí” - Everything Is Noise
content:
Release date: September 11, 2026 | Dark Descent Records/Me Saco Un Ojo Records | Bandcamp | Instagram As much as I love tracking down all sorts of weird, off-the-wall death metal, sometimes I just feel like dipping into a band that does the sound the classic way and does it well. Czechia’s Sněť is exactly that type of band. While I was a little slow on the draw in checking them out, their debut album Mokvání v okovech made quite a splash among my circles of metalhead friends. It’s been a long five years since then, so the hype was palpable when Sněť announced their sophomore V bažinách vědomí. And hey, you don’t want to be late to the party a second time, right? Several listens in, and friends, I can assure you all; Sněť‘s return is plain gross in the absolute best of ways. The band is positively awash in that old 90’s death metal power, laying down mordant tremolo riffs, chunky grooves, and the odd dip into queasy doom drudge that has festered into a fine vintage since the genre’s initial surge. The solos are blazing, the vocals could rumble the foundations of the local mausoleum, and the putrid atmosphere is cloyingly dense while still sounding clear enough for every instrument to shine. V bažinách vědomí wastes no time conjuring a vile climate with the grooving stomp of opener “Tíha světů”. A lumbering, heavy intro gives way to a more nimble verse where riffs ooze along just like they did on the classics. “Kladivo ve tmě” takes on a snappier pace building to some eerily echoing, while “Natur” is even more upfront and forceful. To their credit, Sněť also knows when to let off the gas, as the more doomy, dread-leaden “Ve stínu slunce” proves. That’s also a great song in particular to point out that Sněť likewise understands an old adage from the authority on all metal Fenriz; all the best classic death metal knew it had to be just a little bit weird. “Ve stinu slunce” manages that with its strange acoustic guitar and whispered spoken word outro. There’s a decent number of weird quirks cutting the putrid fury of V bažinách vědomí. The crackling fire and forest sounds of “Natur”. The buzzing intro of “Moskyt”, which I assume was named after the world’s most vile and evil bloodsucker. The chanted invocation of “Znetvořená panna” and weird chirps that close it. Sněť may be walking some well trodden trenches across V bažinách vědomí, but they certainly know how to still leave their own twist on things. As for classic death metal tropes; they’re abundant. Sheer fiery aggression dominates many of the album’s tracks, but it always feels fun in that delightful old school way. Do you dig that old style of indiscernible but weirdly cool cover art? V bažinách vědomí has you covered. A gross but still legible logo? Sněť‘s got one of the better ones! A grimy production that feels weirdly comprehensible despite the muddy grave soil that it’s caked in. Yep, you’ll find it here. I feel like it’s not the easiest to elucidate V bažinách vědomí‘s qualities without just running through a list of what makes old school death metal a perennial delight, but then… that’s kind of just Sněť‘s deal. They’re a band of capable, talented musicians who want to write death metal the way that it won all our hearts in the past. They’re not looking to reinvent the wheel, just to give it their own unique tread (and maybe a couple more sharp edges than engineers would advise). The fact that a band like Sněť can still roll into the decrepit old mortuary of old school death metal and still find an idiosyncratic way to dress the place up is honestly impressive. Death metal just ain’t dying, and I reckon it’s thanks to bands like Sněť that we can say that. May the rotting never cease.
